titleText.es: La vida es demasiado corta para las páginas man, y a veces mucho más corta sin ellas.
titleText.en: Life is too short for man pages, but occasionally much too short without them.
titleText.noteEn: A man page is a Unix-style software manual opened with the command man. RTFM is a rude computing initialism meaning “read the fucking manual.”

regions.labelEs: ¿HOLA, EL 112? ¡ACABO DE INTENTAR TOSTAR ALGO DE PAN Y LA TOSTADORA HA SACADO UN ARMA Y ME LA HA CLAVADO EN LA CARA!

excludedUnits.rationale: 112 is the emergency telephone number used in Spain and elsewhere in Europe, not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Acabo de marks intentar as an action that happened just now, and intentar stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Intentar names the attempt, and tostar follows directly in its unchanged dictionary form.
Algo de gives an unspecified amount, and pan names the substance.
Ha is the helper, and sacado is sacar's completed-action form.
Ha is the helper, and clavado is clavar's completed-action form.

regions.labelEs: ¿SE HA LEÍDO PRIMERO LA PÁGINA MAN DE LA TOSTADORA?

excludedUnits.rationale: man is the Unix command and borrowed technical label for a manual page, not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Ha is the present helper, and leído is leer's completed-action form.
Se matches formal “you” here and adds the read-through nuance to the completed verb phrase ha leído.

regions.labelEs: BUENO, NO, PERO TODO LO QUE QUERÍA ERA...

applications.explanationEn: Bueno softens and delays the reluctant answer before the speaker says no.
Todo lo que marks the full extent of the desire, quería places that desire in the past, and era is the past form of ser that would introduce the complete answer before the interruption.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; introduces a numbered service
cards.noteEn: Spanish can use el before a number that names a masculine service or line. English often uses the number alone.

cards.answerEn: I have just (done something), as part of acabo de
cards.noteEn: Acabo is a form of acabar, which normally means “to finish.” When it is followed by de and an unchanged action verb, the three-part pattern says that the action happened just now.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that an action happened just now?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of acabar, then de, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The final verb stays in its basic -ar, -er, or -ir form. Acabo de means “I have just,” acaba de means “he, she, or formal you has just,” and acabamos de means “we have just.” This pattern talks about recent time; it does not mean literally finishing the later action.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links acabar to a just-completed action
cards.noteEn: In acabar de plus an unchanged action verb, de is required even though natural English does not translate it separately.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone tries to do an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of intentar followed directly by the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: No linking preposition is needed between the two verbs. Intento abrir means “I try to open,” and intentamos salir means “we try to leave.” The attempted action stays in its basic -ar, -er, or -ir form.

example.en: We try to open the window.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “some” or “a bit of” a substance or uncounted thing?
cards.answerEn: Use algo de followed by the thing or substance.
cards.noteEn: Algo normally means “something,” but algo de before a noun describes an unspecified amount. It is especially common with substances and broad categories: algo de agua, algo de tiempo, algo de ayuda.

cards.answerEn: of; or no separate English word, linking an amount to what it measures
cards.noteEn: After a quantity expression, de introduces the substance or thing being measured. English uses “of” in expressions such as a lot of or the amount of, but may leave de untranslated in others, such as un poco de agua, “a little water.”

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: Sacado is the completed-action form of sacar. With a form of haber, it describes something that has been taken or pulled out.

example.es: Han sacado las cajas del coche.
example.en: They have taken the boxes out of the car.

cards.answerEn: a; an (before a feminine noun beginning with a stressed a sound)
cards.noteEn: Some feminine singular nouns beginning with a stressed a sound use un immediately before them. The noun remains feminine, so a describing word is also feminine: un hacha nueva.
Arma is grammatically feminine, but singular el arma and un arma are used because the word begins with a stressed a sound. Its adjectives remain feminine: un arma peligrosa.

cards.answerEn: marks me as the affected person; English often expresses this as “my”
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses me for the affected person and el or la before that person's body part. English usually uses a possessive word instead: me duele la mano means “my hand hurts.”
Clavado is the completed-action form of clavar, “to drive, stick, or plunge something into something else.” With haber, it describes the completed action.

example.es: La rama se ha clavado en la tierra.
example.en: The branch has stuck into the ground.

cards.answerEn: the; used before my body part where English says “my”
cards.noteEn: When a sentence already identifies the affected person with me, Spanish normally uses el or la before that person's body part instead of mi. The same pattern can use te, le, nos, or les for other affected people.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; helps leerse mean “to read through”
cards.noteEn: With actions such as reading or eating, this small word can emphasize carrying the action through over a whole, clearly specified thing. Se is the form used with él, ella, usted, ellos, ellas, or ustedes.

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish emphasize reading, eating, or drinking a whole, clearly specified thing?
cards.answerEn: Choose me, te, se, nos, os, or se to match the person doing the action, and use it with the reading, eating, or drinking verb.
cards.noteEn: These small words can present the action as carried through over the complete book, meal, drink, or stated amount; they do not mean that the person acts on themselves. Compare leer un libro, “read a book,” with leerse un libro, which often suggests reading it through. The small word normally goes before a verb form that shows person and time, as in se leyó; it attaches to an unchanged dictionary form, as in leerse. This completion nuance is not required every time.

example.es: Ana se leyó la novela en dos días.
example.en: Ana read through the novel in two days.

cards.noteEn: Leído is the completed-action form of leer. It follows a form of haber in constructions such as he leído, “I have read.”

example.en: I have already read the message.

cards.noteEn: Primero can describe the first step in an order. In a question about preparation, it can mean “first” or “beforehand.”

cards.answerEn: Unix-like systems provide reference manuals called man pages; RTFM is a rude instruction to read the manual before asking for help
cards.noteEn: The command man opens documentation for commands, programs, file formats, and system calls. RTFM expands to “read the fucking manual.” It is longstanding computing jargon and can sound hostile or dismissive, even when used jokingly.

cards.answerEn: It can mean “well…,” giving the speaker time or softening the reply.
cards.noteEn: Here bueno organizes the conversation rather than describing a person or thing. A pause after it can signal hesitation, reluctance, or a gentle correction.
cards.questionEn: What can bueno mean at the start of an answer when it is not describing something as good?
How does Spanish present what follows as the full answer to what someone wanted, needed, or did?
cards.answerEn: Start with todo lo que, say what the person wanted, needed, or did, then use a form of ser (“to be”) before the full answer.
cards.noteEn: Todo lo que means “all that” or “everything that.” The action changes to show who and when: quería, necesitábamos, hizo. Ser also changes for time, often to es, era, or fue. What follows is presented as the complete answer, whether it contains one item or several.

example.es: Todo lo que necesitamos es tiempo y ayuda.
example.en: All we need is time and help.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Lo combines with que to refer to an idea, action, or whole situation rather than a masculine noun. Together, lo que means “what” or “the thing that.”

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Here que completes lo que, a neutral expression meaning “what” or “the thing that.” It does not refer to a particular masculine or feminine noun.
Quería is a past form of querer used for a desire that existed at that past time. It does not say by itself whether the desire was fulfilled.
Era is a past form of ser used for a background state, description, or ongoing past situation. This form is called the imperfect.
